q-and-k-s1.title: Four mixtures of SO₂, O₂ and SO₃
q-and-k-s1.text: For 2 SO2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2 SO3(g), Kc = 2.80 × 102 at a certain temperature. Four sealed flasks are prepared at that temperature with the starting concentrations below.

q-and-k-s2.title: Making ammonia at high pressure
q-and-k-s2.text: Ammonia forms from nitrogen and hydrogen: N2(g) + 3 H2(g) ⇌ 2 NH3(g). At the temperature of a reactor, Kp = 1.5 × 10−5. At one moment the gas in the reactor has these partial pressures: N2, 10.0 atm; H2, 30.0 atm; NH3, 1.50 atm.

items.q: Calculate the reaction quotient, Q<sub>c</sub>, for flask 1.

mistakes.why: Value: you left out the exponents. Each concentration is raised to the power of its coefficient: [SO₃]² and [SO₂]².
Value: you put the reactants on top. Q is products over reactants, just like K.
Value: you squared [SO₃] but not [SO₂]. Its coefficient is also 2.

items.q: For flask 2, Q<sub>c</sub> = 400. Which way does the net reaction go as flask 2 approaches equilibrium?
options: In reverse, because Q > K: there is too much product for equilibrium.
Forward, because Q > K means the forward reaction is faster.
Forward, because flask 2 holds more SO<sub>3</sub> than SO<sub>2</sub>.
No net reaction, because Q and K are both greater than 1.

why.correct: Compare Q with K. If Q > K, the mixture has too many products relative to reactants, so the net reaction goes in reverse, lowering Q until Q = K.
options: Right: Q = 400 > K = 280. To lower Q, products must turn back into reactants until Q = K.
This flips the rule. Q > K means the ratio of products to reactants is already too high, so the net reaction runs in reverse.
Direction comes from comparing Q with K, not from comparing amounts in the flask.
Being on the same side of 1 means nothing. The flask is at equilibrium only when Q equals K.

items.q: Which flask is already at equilibrium when it is prepared?
options: Flask 3
Flask 1
Flask 2
Flask 4

why.correct: A mixture is at equilibrium when Q = K. Only flask 3 has Q ≈ 280.
options: Right: Q = (0.118)² / ((0.0500)² × 0.0200) = 278, equal to K = 280 within the precision of the data.
Q = 80.0 for flask 1, well below K, so it will react forward.
Q = 400 for flask 2, above K, so it will react in reverse.
Flask 4 has no SO₃, so Q = 0. It can only react forward.

items.q: What happens in flask 4 after it is prepared?
options: SO<sub>3</sub> forms, because Q = 0 is less than K.
Nothing, because there is no SO<sub>3</sub> to react.
SO<sub>2</sub> forms, because Q is less than K.
Q is undefined, because [SO<sub>3</sub>] is zero.

why.correct: A mixture with reactants and no products has Q = 0, which is smaller than any K, so it reacts forward.
options: Right: with no product, Q = 0 < K, so the net reaction must go forward.
The forward reaction needs SO₂ and O₂, which are present. Only the reverse reaction lacks a reactant.
Q < K means net forward, which uses SO₂. It cannot form SO₂.
Q can be calculated: zero on top gives Q = 0. Only a zero on the bottom would be a problem.

items.q: A student says flask 1 will react in reverse because it contains the most SO<sub>3</sub>. Which response is best?
options: Disagree: Q = 80.0 is less than K, so flask 1 reacts forward and makes more SO<sub>3</sub>.
Agree: the flask with the most product reacts in reverse.
Disagree: flask 1 is at equilibrium because it has more SO<sub>3</sub> than SO<sub>2</sub>.
Agree: Q = 80.0 is greater than 1, so the net reaction goes in reverse.

why.correct: The ratio, not a single concentration, decides direction. Flask 1 has Q = 80.0 < K = 280, so more SO₃ forms until Q = K.
options: Right: the comparison that matters is Q with K, and Q is below K.
The amount of product alone does not decide direction. What matters is the whole ratio Q compared with K.
Q = 80.0 is not 280, so flask 1 is not at equilibrium.
Q is compared with K, not with 1. Here Q < K, so the net reaction goes forward.

items.q: Which expression is K<sub>p</sub> for this reaction?
options: P<sub>NH₃</sub><sup>2</sup> / (P<sub>N₂</sub> × P<sub>H₂</sub><sup>3</sup>)
[NH<sub>3</sub>]<sup>2</sup> / ([N<sub>2</sub>][H<sub>2</sub>]<sup>3</sup>)
2 P<sub>NH₃</sub> / (P<sub>N₂</sub> × 3 P<sub>H₂</sub>)
(P<sub>N₂</sub> × P<sub>H₂</sub><sup>3</sup>) / P<sub>NH₃</sub><sup>2</sup>

why.correct: K<sub>p</sub> has the same form as K<sub>c</sub>, with partial pressures in place of concentrations: products over reactants, each to the power of its coefficient.
options: Right: partial pressures of products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient.
This is K<sub>c</sub>. Square brackets mean molar concentrations; K<sub>p</sub> uses partial pressures.
Coefficients become exponents, not multipliers.
This is upside down: products go on top.

items.q: Calculate Q<sub>p</sub> for the gas in the reactor at that moment.

mistakes.why: Value: you did not cube the pressure of H₂. Its coefficient is 3.
Value: you left out the exponents. Raise each pressure to the power of its coefficient.
Value: you inverted the expression. Products go on top.

items.q: Q<sub>p</sub> for the reactor gas is 8.33 × 10<sup>−6</sup>. What happens to the partial pressure of NH<sub>3</sub> as the gas approaches equilibrium?
options: It increases, because Q<sub>p</sub> < K<sub>p</sub>.
It decreases, because Q<sub>p</sub> < K<sub>p</sub>.
It stays the same, because both values are much less than 1.
It decreases, because there is far more H<sub>2</sub> than NH<sub>3</sub>.

why.correct: Q<sub>p</sub> < K<sub>p</sub> means too little product for equilibrium, so the net reaction goes forward and P<sub>NH₃</sub> rises until Q<sub>p</sub> = K<sub>p</sub>.
options: Right: 8.33 × 10⁻⁶ < 1.5 × 10⁻⁵, so the net reaction goes forward and makes NH₃.
Q < K means net forward, which makes NH₃. This mixes up the rule.
Q and K are compared with each other, not with 1. They differ by almost a factor of 2.
Direction comes from comparing Q with K, not from which gas has the higher pressure.

items.q: A student calculates Q<sub>p</sub> using the moles of each gas in the reactor in place of the partial pressures. What is wrong with this approach?
options: K<sub>p</sub> uses partial pressures, so Q<sub>p</sub> has to as well.
Moles are fine, because Q<sub>p</sub> depends on the ratio and not the quantity used.
Moles are fine, as long as the student uses the coefficients as exponents.
Q<sub>p</sub> should use the concentrations in brackets, as K<sub>c</sub> does.

why.correct: Q is only meaningful next to the K of the same form: Q<sub>c</sub> with K<sub>c</sub> (molarities), Q<sub>p</sub> with K<sub>p</sub> (partial pressures in atm).
options: Right: Q and K can only be compared if they are built from the same kind of quantity.
With exponents that do not cancel (2 on top, 4 in total on the bottom), changing the quantity changes the value of Q.
The exponents are right, but moles are not pressures. The result cannot be compared with K<sub>p</sub>.
Concentrations belong in Q<sub>c</sub>, compared with K<sub>c</sub>. For K<sub>p</sub>, use partial pressures without brackets.

items.q: Which is the equilibrium constant expression for CaCO<sub>3</sub>(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO<sub>2</sub>(g)?
options: K<sub>c</sub> = [CO<sub>2</sub>]
K<sub>c</sub> = [CaO][CO<sub>2</sub>] / [CaCO<sub>3</sub>]
K<sub>c</sub> = [CaO] / [CaCO<sub>3</sub>]
K<sub>c</sub> = 1 / [CO<sub>2</sub>]

why.correct: Pure solids and pure liquids do not appear in K or Q, because their concentration is fixed by their density. Only gases and dissolved species are included.
options: Right: the two pure solids are left out, leaving only the gas.
Pure solids are left out of K: their "concentration" does not change however much solid is present.
This keeps the two solids and drops the gas, the opposite of the rule.
CO₂ is a product, so it goes on top.

items.q: For Zn(s) + Cu<sup>2+</sup>(aq) ⇌ Zn<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + Cu(s), which species appear in the denominator of the expression for K<sub>c</sub>? Select all that apply.
options: Cu<sup>2+</sup>(aq)
Zn<sup>2+</sup>(aq)
Zn(s)
Cu(s)

why.correct: K<sub>c</sub> = [Zn²⁺] / [Cu²⁺]. Only Cu²⁺ is in the denominator; the solid metals are left out.
options: Right: a dissolved reactant, so it is in the denominator.
Zn²⁺ is a dissolved product, so it is in the numerator, not the denominator.
Zn is a reactant, but a pure solid is left out of K entirely.
A pure solid is left out of K.

items.q: Which is the expression for K<sub>c</sub> for CH<sub>3</sub>COOH(aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O(l) ⇌ CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>(aq) + H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>(aq)?
options: [CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>][H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] / [CH<sub>3</sub>COOH]
[CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>][H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] / ([CH<sub>3</sub>COOH][H<sub>2</sub>O])
[CH<sub>3</sub>COOH] / ([CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>][H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>])
[CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>] + [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] − [CH<sub>3</sub>COOH]

why.correct: Write products over reactants and leave out pure liquids such as the solvent water.
options: Right: water is the liquid solvent, so it is left out.
Liquid water is the solvent; its concentration barely changes, so it is left out of K.
This is upside down. Products go in the numerator.
Concentrations in K are multiplied and divided, never added or subtracted.

items.q: For H<sub>2</sub>(g) + I<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 HI(g), a mixture holds [H<sub>2</sub>] = 0.0150 M, [I<sub>2</sub>] = 0.0300 M and [HI] = 0.0900 M. Calculate Q<sub>c</sub>.

mistakes.why: Value: [HI] must be squared, because its coefficient is 2.
Value: you multiplied [HI] by 2. The coefficient is an exponent: square [HI].
Value: you inverted the expression. Products go on top.

items.q: For a reaction, K = 4.0 × 10<sup>3</sup>. A mixture has Q = 2.5 × 10<sup>4</sup>. Which statement is correct?
options: Q > K, so reactants form until Q falls to K.
Q > K, so products form until Q rises to K.
Q < K, so products form until Q rises to K.
The mixture is at equilibrium, because Q and K are both large.

why.correct: Q > K: the mixture holds too much product. The net reaction runs in reverse, which lowers Q, until Q = K.
options: Right: 25,000 > 4,000. The net reverse reaction lowers the product-to-reactant ratio until Q = K.
Making more product would raise Q further from K. The net reaction must go the other way.
Compare the powers of ten: 10⁴ is larger than 10³, so Q > K.
At equilibrium Q equals K. Here Q is more than six times K.

items.q: Put the steps for predicting which way a mixture will react in order.
options: Write the expression for Q from the balanced equation, leaving out pure solids and liquids.
Substitute the concentrations (or partial pressures) present right now.
Compare the value of Q with the value of K at the same temperature.
Conclude: Q < K net forward; Q > K net reverse; Q = K at equilibrium.

why.correct: Q has the same form as K but uses the current amounts. Comparing the two tells you which way the system must go to reach equilibrium.

items.q: What is the difference between Q and K for the same reaction at the same temperature?
options: Q uses the amounts present at any moment; K uses the amounts at equilibrium.
Q uses reactants over products; K uses products over reactants.
Q is used for gases; K is used for solutions.
Q includes solids and liquids; K leaves them out.

why.correct: Q and K have identical expressions. K is the value at equilibrium, which is fixed at a given temperature; Q is the value right now, which changes as the reaction runs.
options: Right: same expression, but K is the special value Q takes at equilibrium.
Both are products over reactants. Only the moment at which the amounts are measured differs.
Either can be written for gases (K<sub>p</sub>, Q<sub>p</sub> with pressures) or solutions (K<sub>c</sub>, Q<sub>c</sub>).
Solids and pure liquids are left out of both, so the two can be compared.

items.q: For 2 NO(g) + Cl<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 NOCl(g), K<sub>c</sub> = 4.6 × 10<sup>4</sup> at a certain temperature. A mixture at that temperature has [NO] = 0.020 M and [Cl<sub>2</sub>] = 0.010 M. Calculate the [NOCl] for which this mixture would be at equilibrium.

mistakes.why: Value: you found [NOCl]² but did not take the square root. [NOCl] is squared in the expression, so finish with a square root.
Value: [NO] must be squared, because its coefficient is 2.

why.correct: At equilibrium Q = K: [NOCl]² / ([NO]²[Cl₂]) = 4.6 × 10⁴. So [NOCl]² = 4.6 × 10⁴ × (0.020)² × 0.010 = 0.184, and [NOCl] = √0.184 = 0.43 M.
